course.title: Mathematical Modelling
course.tagline: Turn real-world problems into mathematics, from first assumptions to research-grade models.
course.description:
- **Level 1: Foundations of Mathematical Modelling**: Understand the philosophy, principles and processes involved in converting real-world problems into mathematical models.
- **Level 2: Mathematical Tools for Modelling**: Develop the mathematical foundations required to construct and analyse models.
- **Level 3: Static and Deterministic Models**: Develop models that describe systems at a particular point in time or under predictable conditions.
- **Level 4: Dynamic Models and Differential Equations**: Understand systems that evolve or change over time.
- **Level 5: Probability, Statistics and Stochastic Models**: Develop mathematical models for systems involving uncertainty, randomness and unpredictable events.
- **Level 6: Computational and Numerical Modelling**: Learn how to implement mathematical models using computational tools and numerical methods.
- **Level 7: Advanced Mathematical Modelling**: Develop the ability to model complex systems using advanced mathematical structures and techniques.
- **Level 8: Applied and Research-Oriented Mathematical Modelling**: Apply mathematical modelling to complex real-world problems and develop independent research capabilities.

concepts.title: Introduction to mathematical modelling
concepts.summary: Turn messy real-world questions into equations you can solve and act on.

blocks.title: Level 1: Foundations of Mathematical Modelling
blocks.md:
Understand the philosophy, principles and processes involved in converting real-world problems into mathematical models.

By the end of this level you should be able to:
- Identify real-world problems suitable for mathematical modelling
- Translate practical problems into mathematical language
- Identify dependent and independent variables
- Formulate appropriate assumptions
- Understand the strengths and limitations of different model types

## What is a mathematical model?

A **mathematical model** is a simplified description of a real system written in mathematical language: variables, equations, inequalities or rules. We build models because the real system is too expensive, too slow, too dangerous or simply impossible to experiment on directly. A retailer cannot open fifty trial shops to find the best price, and a health agency cannot let an epidemic run just to see what happens.

A model links **inputs** (things we know or control) to **outputs** (things we want to predict or decide):

$$\text{output} = f(\text{inputs};\ \text{parameters})$$

## What models are used for

- **Explain**: why do queues at a supermarket suddenly get long?
- **Predict**: how many patients will need a hospital bed next week?
- **Decide**: what price, order size or staffing level is best?
- **Explore "what if"**: what happens to profit if energy costs rise by 20%?

## The modelling cycle

Modelling is not a one-shot calculation. It is a loop: describe the real problem, make assumptions, formulate the mathematics, solve it, interpret the answer in real-world terms, and check it against reality. If the check fails, you revise the assumptions and go round again.

## Is a problem suitable for modelling?

Good candidates have a clear question, quantities that can be measured or estimated, and relationships between them that can be described (even roughly). "Should we hire a third barista on Saturdays?" is a modelling question. "Is our brand cool?" is not, until you turn it into something measurable.

blocks.title: Break-even point for a coffee cart
blocks.problem: A coffee cart sells each cup for £3.00. Ingredients and cups cost £1.20 per drink, and the pitch rent, insurance and wages cost £270 per day regardless of sales. How many cups must be sold each day to break even? On a typical day the cart sells 120 cups. What does the model say?
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** Let $q$ be the number of cups sold per day. Revenue is $3q$, variable cost is $1.2q$ and fixed cost is 270, so daily profit is

$$P(q) = 3q - 1.2q - 270 = 1.8q - 270.$$

Assumptions: price and unit cost stay fixed, and every cup made is sold.

**Solve.** Break-even means $P(q) = 0$:

$$1.8q = 270 \quad\Rightarrow\quad q = 150.$$

At $q = 120$: $P(120) = 1.8 \times 120 - 270 = 216 - 270 = -54$.

**Interpret.** The cart needs 150 cups a day to cover its costs. At 120 cups it loses about £54 per day. The owner could raise the price, cut fixed costs or move to a busier pitch. The model makes the size of the gap explicit, which is what turns a vague worry into a decision.

blocks.title: The model is not the reality
blocks.md: A model is a deliberate simplification. The coffee cart model ignores weather, wasted milk and the fact that a higher price would probably sell fewer cups. That is fine as long as you **remember** what was left out and check whether it matters for the decision you are making.

blocks.question: Which of these questions is best suited to a mathematical model as stated?
options: Is our logo more attractive than a competitor’s?
How many checkout staff are needed so that 90% of customers wait less than 5 minutes?
Which colour do customers like best?
blocks.explanation: It has a clear, measurable target (waiting time), quantities that can be estimated (arrival and service rates) and a decision variable (number of staff).

cards.back: A simplified representation of a real system using mathematical objects such as variables, equations and rules.
A quantity fed into the model: known data or a decision we control.
What the model predicts or recommends.
Problem → assumptions → formulation → solution → interpretation → validation → revision.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a mathematical model?
options: A simplified mathematical representation of a real system built for a purpose
An exact copy of a real system in equations
Any formula found in a textbook
A computer program that collects data
questions.explanation: Models are purposeful simplifications. They are never exact copies, and a formula only becomes a model when it represents a real system.

questions.prompt: Once a model has been solved, the modelling process is complete.
questions.explanation: Solving is only one stage. The answer must be interpreted in real-world terms and validated against data, and the model is often revised and solved again.

questions.prompt: A food truck sells meals at £8 each, each meal costs £3 to make and fixed costs are £400 per day. How many meals per day are needed to break even?
questions.explanation: Profit is $8q - 3q - 400 = 5q - 400$. Setting this to zero gives $q = 80$.

questions.prompt: Which of these are typical purposes of a mathematical model?
options: Choosing the best order quantity for a warehouse
Exploring what happens to profit if costs rise
Guaranteeing that a forecast will be exactly right
questions.explanation: Models predict, support decisions and explore scenarios. No model can guarantee an exact forecast, because every model simplifies reality.

questions.prompt: In the modelling cycle, what usually comes immediately after solving the mathematical problem?
options: Interpreting the solution in real-world terms
questions.explanation: After solving, you translate the mathematical answer back into the language of the original problem, then validate it.

questions.prompt: A model predicts a daily profit of $P = 1.8q - 270$ (in £). What is the profit when 200 cups are sold?

concepts.title: History and evolution of mathematical modelling
concepts.summary: From Newton’s laws to epidemic curves: the models that shaped how we think.

blocks.md:
## Why history matters to a modeller

Many models used today are direct descendants of a handful of classic ideas. Knowing where they came from shows you **which questions they were built to answer** and which assumptions they carry with them.

## Key milestones

- **1687, Isaac Newton**, _Principia_: laws of motion and universal gravitation. Motion is described by how quantities change, $F = ma$, which led to modelling with differential equations.
- **1798, Thomas Malthus**, _An Essay on the Principle of Population_: population tends to grow geometrically (by a constant factor) while food supply grows arithmetically (by a constant amount), so population eventually outruns food.
- **1838, Pierre-François Verhulst**: the logistic model, in which growth slows as a population approaches a carrying capacity $K$.
- **1920s, Alfred Lotka and Vito Volterra**: predator–prey equations. Volterra was motivated by changes in Adriatic fish catches after the First World War.
- **1922, Lewis Fry Richardson**, _Weather Prediction by Numerical Process_: forecasting weather by solving the equations of the atmosphere numerically, done by hand.
- **1927, William Kermack and Anderson McKendrick**: the SIR model for epidemics, splitting a population into Susceptible, Infected and Recovered groups.
- **1950**: the first computer weather forecasts, run on the ENIAC computer by Jule Charney, Ragnar Fjørtoft and John von Neumann.
- **1963, Edward Lorenz**: a simple weather model shows _sensitive dependence on initial conditions_ (chaos), which puts a limit on long-range forecasting.

## Three classic equations

Malthusian growth:

$$\frac{dP}{dt} = rP$$

Lotka–Volterra predator–prey ($x$ prey, $y$ predators):

$$\frac{dx}{dt} = \alpha x - \beta xy, \qquad \frac{dy}{dt} = \delta xy - \gamma y$$

Kermack–McKendrick SIR:

$$\frac{dS}{dt} = -\frac{\beta SI}{N}, \quad \frac{dI}{dt} = \frac{\beta SI}{N} - \gamma I, \quad \frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I$$

## The big shift: computers

Before computers, models had to be solvable by hand, so modellers simplified heavily. Since the mid-twentieth century, numerical simulation has made it possible to use far richer models, from global climate to financial risk.

blocks.prompt: Put these modelling milestones in chronological order (earliest first).
items: Newton publishes the laws of motion in Principia
Malthus argues population outgrows food supply
Verhulst proposes the logistic growth model
Richardson attempts a numerical weather forecast by hand
Kermack and McKendrick publish the SIR epidemic model
First computer weather forecast on ENIAC
Lorenz discovers sensitive dependence in a weather model

blocks.title: Malthus in numbers
blocks.problem: A country has 10 million people, growing by 2% per year. Its food production currently feeds 10 million people and increases by enough to feed an extra 0.5 million people each year. Using Malthus’s assumptions, how long does the population take to double, and roughly when does population overtake food supply?
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** Population grows geometrically and food arithmetically (in millions, $t$ in years):

$$P(t) = 10(1.02)^t, \qquad F(t) = 10 + 0.5t.$$

**Solve.** Doubling: $(1.02)^t = 2$, so

$$t = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.02} = \frac{0.6931}{0.0198} \approx 35 \text{ years}.$$

Comparing values: at $t = 50$, $P \approx 26.9$ and $F = 35$, so food is still ahead. At $t = 82$, $P \approx 50.7$ and $F = 51.0$. At $t = 83$, $P \approx 51.7$ and $F = 51.5$. The crossover happens between years 82 and 83.

**Interpret.** Early on the linear food supply grows faster, but any geometric growth eventually beats any arithmetic growth. Malthus’s conclusion depends entirely on these two assumptions. In practice, technology raised food output far faster than a fixed annual amount, which is why his prediction did not come true in the way he expected. The structure of his argument, comparing growth laws, is still a core modelling idea.

blocks.prompt: Match each classic model to the question it was built to answer.

pairs.right: How do objects move under forces?
Will population outgrow the food supply?
Why do predator and prey numbers cycle?
How does an epidemic rise and fall?
Can weather be forecast by calculation?

blocks.title: Old assumptions travel with old models
blocks.md: Classic models are often reused without re-reading their assumptions. The basic SIR model assumes everyone mixes equally and recovered people stay immune. That is reasonable for a short outbreak in a town but not for a disease where immunity wanes, or where schools and workplaces mix very differently. Always check whether a borrowed model’s assumptions fit your situation.

questions.prompt: Which pair developed the SIR model of epidemics in 1927?
questions.explanation: William Kermack and Anderson McKendrick published the compartmental SIR model in 1927.

questions.prompt: According to Malthus, how do population and food supply tend to grow?
questions.explanation: Malthus argued population multiplies by a constant factor each period while food increases by a constant amount, so population eventually outruns food.

questions.prompt: Lorenz’s work in the 1960s showed that small errors in initial conditions can grow, which limits how far ahead weather can be forecast.
questions.explanation: Lorenz found sensitive dependence on initial conditions in a simplified weather model, a founding result of chaos theory.

questions.prompt: In the Lotka–Volterra model $\frac{dx}{dt} = \alpha x - \beta xy$, what does the term $-\beta xy$ represent?
options: Prey migrating away at a constant rate
Prey being eaten, at a rate depending on encounters between prey and predators
questions.explanation: The product $xy$ measures how often prey and predators meet, so $-\beta xy$ is the loss of prey to predation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are well-established milestones in the history of mathematical modelling?
options: Richardson’s attempt at numerical weather prediction by hand (1922)
Lotka and Volterra’s SIR epidemic model (1927)
The first computer weather forecast on ENIAC (1950)
Newton’s publication of the SIR epidemic model
questions.explanation: Richardson (1922) and the ENIAC forecast (1950) are genuine milestones. The SIR model is due to Kermack and McKendrick (1927); Lotka and Volterra worked on predator–prey models, and Newton published laws of motion and gravitation in 1687.

questions.prompt: A population grows by 2% per year. To the nearest whole year, how many years does it take to double?
questions.explanation: $t = \ln 2 / \ln 1.02 \approx 0.6931 / 0.0198 \approx 35$ years.

concepts.title: Mathematics as a language for describing reality
concepts.summary: Learn to translate everyday phrases like “proportional to” into precise maths.

blocks.md:
## Why a language?

Words are flexible but ambiguous. "Sales are rising fast" could mean 2% or 200%. Mathematics forces you to say exactly **what changes, by how much, and depending on what**. Once a statement is written mathematically, you can compute with it, test it against data and share it without misunderstanding.

## A translation dictionary

- "$y$ **increases by** 5 for each extra unit of $x$" → $y = a + 5x$
- "$y$ is **proportional to** $x$" → $y = kx$
- "$y$ is **inversely proportional to** $x$" → $y = \dfrac{k}{x}$
- "**at least** 40 staff" → $s \ge 40$; "**no more than** £500" → $c \le 500$
- "grows by 3% each year" → $P_{n+1} = 1.03\,P_n$
- "the **rate of change** of $P$" → $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$
- "the growth rate is proportional to the population" →

$$\frac{dP}{dt} = kP$$

## Grammar of a model

- **Nouns** are quantities: price, number of customers, temperature. Give each a symbol and a unit.
- **Verbs** are relationships: "depends on", "increases", "balances". These become equations, inequalities and functions.
- **Conditions** are constraints and starting values: "the budget is £10,000", "initially 200 people are infected".

Writing the model is mostly careful reading: underline every quantity, decide what each symbol means, then turn each sentence into one mathematical statement.

blocks.prompt: Match each phrase to its mathematical translation.

pairs.left: Travel time is inversely proportional to speed
Demand falls by 20 units for each £1 price rise
A balance grows by 1% each month
Population grows at a rate proportional to its size

steps.title: Read and underline quantities
steps.md: A loan of **£5,000** charges **1% interest per month**, and the borrower repays **£200 per month**.

steps.title: Name each quantity with a symbol and unit
steps.md: Let $B_n$ be the balance (£) after $n$ months. The interest rate is $0.01$ per month and the repayment is £200 per month.

steps.title: Turn each sentence into a statement
steps.md:
Each month the balance gains 1% interest, then £200 is repaid:

$$B_{n+1} = 1.01\,B_n - 200, \qquad B_0 = 5000.$$

steps.title: Check that it reads back correctly
steps.md: Read the equation aloud in words: "next month’s balance is this month’s balance plus 1%, minus 200." It matches the original sentence.

blocks.title: How fast is the loan paid off?
blocks.problem: Using the loan model $B_{n+1} = 1.01\,B_n - 200$ with $B_0 = 5000$, find the balance after 1 and 2 months. Is the loan being paid off, and roughly how much of each payment goes to interest at the start?
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** The model is already written: $B_{n+1} = 1.01\,B_n - 200$, $B_0 = 5000$.

**Solve.**

$$B_1 = 1.01 \times 5000 - 200 = 5050 - 200 = 4850$$

$$B_2 = 1.01 \times 4850 - 200 = 4898.50 - 200 = 4698.50$$

**Interpret.** The balance falls by £150 in month 1 and by £151.50 in month 2. In the first month £50 of the £200 payment is interest and £150 reduces the debt. Because interest is charged on a shrinking balance, more of each payment goes to the debt over time. If the repayment were only £50, the balance would never fall. The equation makes that threshold obvious: repayment must exceed $0.01 B_n$.

blocks.title: Per cent versus percentage points
blocks.md: "Interest rises from 4% to 5%" is a rise of **1 percentage point** but a **25% increase** in the rate. Mixing these up is one of the most common translation errors in business and policy models. Write the rule as an equation, $r_{\text{new}} = r + 0.01$ or $r_{\text{new}} = 1.25r$, and the ambiguity disappears.

blocks.question: Which equation says "the number of complaints $N$ is proportional to the square of the waiting time $w$"?
blocks.explanation: Proportional to means "equals a constant times", so $N = kw^2$.

questions.prompt: Which equation translates "the time $t$ to finish a job is inversely proportional to the number of workers $n$"?
questions.explanation: Inversely proportional means $t = k/n$: doubling the workers halves the time.

questions.prompt: A delivery firm needs "at least 12 drivers on every shift". If $d$ is the number of drivers, which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: "At least 12" includes 12 itself, so $d \ge 12$.

questions.prompt: A printing job costs $C = 50 + 4q$ pounds for $q$ copies. What is the cost of 20 copies, in pounds?
If an interest rate rises from 4% to 5%, the rate has increased by 1%.
questions.explanation: It has increased by 1 percentage point, which is a 25% increase in the rate itself: $(5 - 4)/4 = 0.25$.

questions.prompt: Which equation says "the rate at which a rumour spreads is proportional to the number of people $R$ who already know it"?
questions.explanation: A rate of change written as $dR/dt$ that is proportional to $R$ gives $dR/dt = kR$.

questions.prompt: A café’s daily profit is described as "£2 per coffee sold minus £150 fixed costs, and the café can make no more than 300 coffees a day". Which statements belong in the model? ($q$ = coffees sold)
questions.explanation: Profit is $2q - 150$, capacity gives $q \le 300$, and you cannot sell a negative number of coffees, so $q \ge 0$ is an implied condition. $P = 150q - 2$ swaps the roles of the numbers, and nothing in the description limits sales to 150.

concepts.title: Types of mathematical models
concepts.summary: A map of model types, and how to pick the right kind for a problem.

blocks.md:
## Why classify models?

Knowing the type of a model tells you which mathematical tools you will need, what kind of answer you will get, and what can go wrong. Choosing a type is one of the first decisions in any modelling project.

## Four key contrasts

Every mathematical model can be described along several independent dimensions:

- **Deterministic vs stochastic**: does the model include randomness? A deterministic model always gives the same output for the same inputs; a stochastic model gives a range of possible outcomes with probabilities.
- **Static vs dynamic**: does time play a role? A static model describes one moment or an equilibrium; a dynamic model tracks how things change over time.
- **Linear vs nonlinear**: are the relationships straight-line (proportional changes and sums) or curved (powers, products, thresholds)?
- **Continuous vs discrete**: do variables (or time) change smoothly, or in separate steps and whole numbers?

## Where the model comes from

- **Mechanistic (theory-driven)** models are built from how the system works: conservation of mass, Newton’s laws, cash in minus cash out.
- **Empirical (data-driven)** models are fitted to observed patterns without claiming to explain them, such as a trend line through past sales.

Most real models mix both: a mechanistic structure with parameters estimated from data.

## One problem, many models

The **same** real problem can be modelled in different ways. Daily visitors to a website could be a fixed average (deterministic, static), a random number each day (stochastic), or a growing trend (dynamic). The type describes the model you chose, not the problem itself.

cards.back: No randomness: the same inputs always give the same output. Example: break-even analysis.
Includes random variation; outputs are distributions. Example: simulating random customer arrivals.
No time evolution; a snapshot or equilibrium. Example: a fixed-price profit calculation.
State changes over time. Example: monthly growth of a savings account.
Effects add up and scale proportionally. Example: $C = 50 + 4q$.
Curves, products or thresholds. Example: revenue $R = p(1000 - 20p)$.
Smooth change, often with differential equations. Example: $dP/dt = rP$.
Step-by-step change or whole-number quantities. Example: $P_{n+1} = 1.05P_n$.

blocks.title: Classifying a bank queue simulation
blocks.problem:
A bank models its lunchtime queue minute by minute. In each minute, the number of arriving customers is drawn at random from past data, each open counter serves one customer per minute, and the queue length is updated:

$$Q_{n+1} = \max(0,\ Q_n + A_n - c)$$

where $A_n$ is the random number of arrivals in minute $n$ and $c$ is the number of open counters. Classify this model on all four contrasts.
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** Look at each feature of the equation in turn.

**Solve (classify).**
- **Stochastic**: $A_n$ is random, so running the model twice gives different queues.
- **Dynamic**: $Q$ evolves from one minute to the next.
- **Discrete**: time moves in one-minute steps and the queue is a whole number of people.
- **Nonlinear**: the $\max(0, \cdot)$ creates a kink, because the queue cannot be negative. Without it the update would be linear.

**Interpret.** Because the model is stochastic, the bank should run it many times and look at the spread, for example "with 3 counters the queue exceeds 10 people on 15% of days", rather than trusting a single run. Its discrete, step-by-step form makes it easy to simulate in a spreadsheet.

blocks.prompt: Match each description to the model type it points to.

pairs.left: Rerunning with identical inputs gives a different answer
No time variable: describes a single moment
Tracks a quantity hour by hour
A curve fitted to past data without explaining why
Built from a balance law: water in minus water out

blocks.title: Labels describe the model, not reality
blocks.md: Students often ask "is a population stochastic or deterministic?" Reality is neither: it is the **model** that is one or the other. Choose the type that fits your question. Thousands of bacteria can be modelled deterministically; five endangered rhinos usually need a stochastic model, because chance events dominate small numbers.

blocks.question: A model calculates the monthly mortgage payment from the loan size, interest rate and term, with no randomness. Which description fits best?
blocks.explanation: There is no randomness (deterministic), and the formula comes from how interest and repayments work (mechanistic), not from fitting data.

questions.prompt: A weather service runs its forecast model 50 times with slightly different starting conditions to estimate the probability of rain. What type of model approach is this?
questions.explanation: Running many versions with random variation and summarising the spread produces probabilities, which is a stochastic (ensemble) approach.

questions.prompt: The same real-world problem can be represented by both a deterministic model and a stochastic model.
questions.explanation: Model type is a modelling choice. Daily demand can be modelled as a fixed average or as a random variable, depending on the question.

questions.prompt: Which model is empirical rather than mechanistic?
options: Tank level = water in − water out
A straight line fitted to the last 24 months of sales
Account balance from interest and deposits
questions.explanation: A fitted trend line describes a pattern in data without explaining the mechanism. The others are built from how the system works.

questions.prompt: The model $P_{n+1} = 1.05\,P_n$ for yearly town population (no randomness) is which of the following?
questions.explanation: No randomness (deterministic), it changes over time (dynamic), it updates in yearly steps (discrete) and the next value is a constant multiple of the current one (linear). It is not stochastic.

questions.prompt: Which contrast is about whether time plays a role in the model?
questions.explanation: Static models describe a snapshot; dynamic models describe change over time.

concepts.title: Deterministic vs stochastic models
concepts.summary: When is an average good enough, and when does randomness change the answer?

blocks.md:
## The key question: does chance matter?

A **deterministic** model has no randomness: given the same inputs it always produces the same output. A **stochastic** model includes random variables, so its output is a range of outcomes with probabilities.

Deterministic, for example a bakery that always sells 100 loaves:

$$\text{Profit} = 2.5 \times 100 - 1 \times 100 = 150$$

Stochastic, for example demand $D$ that is random:

$$\text{Profit} = 2.5 \times \min(D,\ \text{baked}) - 1 \times \text{baked}$$

The stochastic answer is a **distribution**, summarised by an **expected value** (average outcome) and a measure of spread or risk:

$$E[X] = \sum_i x_i\, p_i$$

## When to choose which

- **Deterministic** works well when variation is small compared with the quantities involved, when you need a quick first answer, or when the system is genuinely predictable (loan repayments, a planned production line).
- **Stochastic** is needed when variation drives the decision: stock-outs, queues, insurance claims, small populations, financial risk, or any question phrased as "what is the chance that…?"

Deterministic models are simpler to build and explain. Stochastic models are more realistic about uncertainty but need probability distributions, and are usually solved by simulation (the Monte Carlo method) or probability theory.

blocks.title: How many loaves should the bakery bake?
blocks.problem: A bakery sells loaves for £2.50 and each costs £1.00 to bake. Unsold loaves are thrown away. Daily demand is 80, 100 or 120 loaves with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25. Compare the deterministic prediction (demand always equals the average) with the stochastic expected profit when baking 100 loaves. Then check baking 80 or 120.
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** Average demand is $0.25(80) + 0.5(100) + 0.25(120) = 100$. With $b$ loaves baked and demand $D$:

$$\text{Profit} = 2.5\min(D, b) - b.$$

**Solve.** Deterministic, with $D = 100$ and $b = 100$: profit $= 250 - 100 = £150$.

Stochastic, with $b = 100$:
- $D = 80$: $2.5(80) - 100 = 100$
- $D = 100$: $250 - 100 = 150$
- $D = 120$: only 100 can be sold, so $150$

$$E[\text{Profit}] = 0.25(100) + 0.5(150) + 0.25(150) = 137.50$$

Baking 120: profits 80, 130 and 180, expected $20 + 65 + 45 = £130$. Baking 80: always sells 80, profit $200 - 80 = £120$.

**Interpret.** The deterministic model overstates profit by £12.50 a day because it ignores the days when loaves go unsold. Among these options, baking 100 is best, with an expected profit of £137.50. Only the stochastic model reveals the risk: on a quarter of days profit drops to £100.

blocks.title: The flaw of averages
blocks.md: Plugging the **average input** into a model does not give the **average output** whenever the model has a kink or curve, like $\min(D, b)$ above. Average demand gave £150, but average profit is only £137.50. This error leads to systematic over-optimism in inventory, project timelines and capacity planning.

items.q: A factory machine fills 1 kg bags with a tiny variation of ±2 g. Deterministic or stochastic?
items.a: Deterministic is fine for costing: the variation is negligible compared with 1 kg. For quality control, though, where the question is about the chance a bag is underweight, a stochastic model is needed.

items.q: An insurer wants to know how much capital to hold so it survives a bad year. Which type?
items.a: Stochastic. The question is about rare, extreme outcomes, which an average cannot capture.

items.q: A city plans water supply for 2 million residents next year. Which type?
items.a: A deterministic model is a reasonable start, because with large numbers individual randomness averages out. Add stochastic rainfall if drought risk matters.

blocks.question: A stochastic model of daily sales is run 1,000 times. What is the most useful output?
options: The result of the first run
Nothing, because random models cannot be used for decisions
The distribution of outcomes, such as the average and the 5th–95th percentile range
blocks.explanation: Stochastic models are judged by the distribution they produce: expected value plus spread or risk.

questions.prompt: A deterministic model run twice with identical inputs always gives identical outputs.
questions.explanation: That is the definition of deterministic: there is no random element.

questions.prompt: Which situation most clearly calls for a stochastic model?
options: Calculating the area of a warehouse floor
Estimating the probability that a call centre’s wait exceeds 10 minutes
Converting a recipe for 4 people into a recipe for 12
Computing the monthly payment on a fixed-rate loan
questions.explanation: The question asks for a probability driven by random call arrivals and durations, which needs randomness in the model.

questions.prompt: A stall’s daily profit is £100 with probability 0.25, £150 with probability 0.5 and £150 with probability 0.25. What is the expected daily profit in pounds?
Demand is random with average 100. A planner puts 100 into a profit model containing $\min(D, b)$ and gets £150. What is the true expected profit most likely to be?
questions.explanation: Because $\min(D, b)$ caps sales on high-demand days but not losses on low-demand days, the expected profit cannot exceed the profit at average demand (the flaw of averages).

questions.prompt: Which are advantages of a deterministic model over a stochastic one?
options: Gives a single clear answer quickly
Captures the risk of rare extreme events
Needs no probability distributions as inputs
questions.explanation: Deterministic models are simpler, faster and need no distributions. Capturing rare extreme events is a strength of stochastic models.

questions.prompt: A wildlife agency models a population of 6 breeding pairs of a rare bird. Why is a stochastic model preferable?
options: Chance events, such as a few failed nests, can dominate the outcome and even cause extinction
questions.explanation: With small numbers, random births and deaths do not average out. A stochastic model can estimate the extinction risk, which an average-based model hides.

concepts.title: Static vs dynamic models
concepts.summary: Snapshot or film? Decide whether time belongs in your model.

blocks.md:
## Snapshot or film?

A **static** model describes a system at one moment, or in a steady state, with no explicit time. A **dynamic** model describes how the **state** of a system changes over time.

Static, for example the total yearly cost of ordering stock in batches of size $Q$:

$$TC(Q) = \frac{DS}{Q} + \frac{HQ}{2}$$

Dynamic, for example a savings balance updated every month:

$$S_{n+1} = (1 + i)\,S_n + d$$

or, in continuous time, a population changing at every instant:

$$\frac{dP}{dt} = rP$$

## The idea of state

A dynamic model has **state variables** (balance, stock level, number infected) and an **update rule** that says how today’s state produces tomorrow’s. You also need an **initial condition**: where the system starts.

## When to choose which

- **Static** suits one-off decisions, long-run averages and equilibria: break-even, optimal order size, a budget allocation.
- **Dynamic** suits questions about **when** and **how fast**: when will the loan be paid off, how quickly will an epidemic peak, how does stock run down after a supplier fails.

A static model can often be read as the **equilibrium** of a dynamic one: the point where the state stops changing.

blocks.title: Static: the economic order quantity
blocks.problem: A shop sells $D = 1200$ printer cartridges a year. Each order costs $S = £50$ in admin and delivery, and holding one cartridge in stock for a year costs $H = £3$. What order size minimises total annual cost, and what is that cost? Use $Q^* = \sqrt{2DS/H}$.
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** Total annual cost is ordering cost plus holding cost:

$$TC(Q) = \frac{DS}{Q} + \frac{HQ}{2}.$$

Assumptions: steady demand, instant delivery, no shortages. Time does not appear: the model describes an average year.

**Solve.**

$$Q^* = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1200 \times 50}{3}} = \sqrt{40000} = 200$$

$$TC(200) = \frac{1200 \times 50}{200} + \frac{3 \times 200}{2} = 300 + 300 = £600$$

**Interpret.** Order 200 cartridges at a time, which is 6 orders a year, for a total cost of £600. At the optimum the ordering and holding costs are equal. Because the model is static, it cannot tell you what happens in a week when a delivery is late. That question needs a dynamic stock model.

blocks.title: Dynamic: stepping a savings account forward

steps.title: State and rule
steps.md:
A saver has $S_0 = £2000$, earns 0.5% interest per month and deposits £100 at the end of each month:

$$S_{n+1} = 1.005\,S_n + 100.$$

steps.title: Interpret
steps.md: Each month the balance grows by a little more than the month before, because interest is earned on earlier interest. The dynamic model answers questions a static one cannot, such as when the balance reaches £5,000.

blocks.title: How a dynamic model runs
nodes: Repeat for the next time step

blocks.title: Static models miss feedback
blocks.md: A static pricing model might say a 10% price rise increases revenue. Over time, though, customers switch to competitors, competitors respond, and demand drifts down month after month. When today’s outcome changes tomorrow’s conditions, a static model can be badly misleading. Ask: "does the system react over time?"

blocks.question: Which question needs a dynamic model?
options: How many weeks until a reservoir runs dry if the drought continues?
What is the break-even sales volume at today’s prices?
What is the area of land needed for 200 solar panels?
Which of three suppliers is cheapest for one order?
blocks.explanation: "How many weeks until" is a question about change over time, so the reservoir level must be tracked as a state.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a dynamic model from a static one?
options: It describes how the state of a system changes over time
questions.explanation: Dynamic means time-dependent. Randomness and nonlinearity are separate contrasts.

questions.prompt: A balance follows $S_{n+1} = 1.005\,S_n + 100$ with $S_0 = 2000$. What is $S_1$ in pounds?
Using $Q^* = \sqrt{2DS/H}$ with $D = 800$ units a year, $S = £25$ per order and $H = £4$ per unit per year, what is the optimal order quantity?
An equilibrium of a dynamic model is a state at which the model stops changing.
questions.explanation: At an equilibrium the update rule returns the same state, so a static model can often be read as the equilibrium of a dynamic one.

questions.prompt: Which of these are needed to run a discrete-time dynamic model?
questions.explanation: You need a starting point and a rule for moving from one step to the next. A distribution is only needed if the model is also stochastic, and the rule can perfectly well be linear.

concepts.title: Linear vs nonlinear models
concepts.summary: Straight lines are easy, but the real world often curves. Know when it matters.

blocks.md:
## Straight lines and curves

In a **linear** model, the output changes by the same amount for each unit change in an input, and the effects of different inputs simply add up. In applied modelling, "linear" usually includes a constant term:

$$y = a + bx \qquad\text{or}\qquad y = a + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2$$

A **nonlinear** model contains anything else: powers, products of variables, exponentials, ratios, thresholds or caps. For example:

$$R = p\,(1000 - 20p), \qquad \frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right), \qquad y = \max(0,\ x - 50)$$

## Why it matters

- **Linear models** are easy to solve, easy to explain and easy to combine. Small changes have proportional effects. Linear programming can optimise thousands of variables at once.
- **Nonlinear models** can show behaviour linear models never can: an optimum in the middle (best price), saturation (market limits), tipping points, and cycles. They are harder to solve and often need numerical methods.

## Spotting nonlinearity

Ask: "If I double the change in the input, does the change in the output double?" Also look for **products of variables** ($xy$), **variables in exponents** ($e^{rt}$), **powers** ($x^2$), and **if/then rules** (tax bands, capacity limits).

Many nonlinear systems look linear over a small range. That is why linear approximations work well locally and fail when stretched.

blocks.title: Finding the best price
blocks.problem: A concert venue finds that at a ticket price of $p$ pounds it sells $q = 1000 - 20p$ tickets. What price maximises ticket revenue? Compare revenue at £25 and £30.
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** Revenue is price times quantity:

$$R(p) = p\,(1000 - 20p) = 1000p - 20p^2.$$

This is nonlinear (quadratic) in $p$, even though demand itself is linear.

**Solve.** Set the derivative to zero:

$$R'(p) = 1000 - 40p = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad p = 25.$$

$R(25) = 25 \times (1000 - 500) = 25 \times 500 = £12{,}500$.

$R(30) = 30 \times (1000 - 600) = 30 \times 400 = £12{,}000$.

**Interpret.** Revenue peaks at £25 a ticket with 500 sold. Raising the price to £30 loses 100 sales and £500 of revenue. A linear way of thinking ("a higher price means more money per ticket, so more revenue") misses this turning point. The curvature is the whole reason an optimum exists.

blocks.prompt: Classify each relationship.

blocks.title: Extrapolating a straight line
blocks.md: A start-up’s users grew by about 2,000 a month for six months, so a linear model predicts 240,000 extra users in ten years. Real adoption usually follows an S-shaped (logistic) curve that flattens as the market saturates. A linear fit that is excellent **inside** the data range can be wildly wrong **outside** it.

blocks.question: A delivery firm’s fuel use is $F = 0.08d$ litres for $d$ km. If the distance doubles, what happens to fuel use?
blocks.explanation: In this linear model fuel is proportional to distance, so doubling $d$ doubles $F$.

questions.prompt: Which of these models are nonlinear?
questions.explanation: $5x^2$ is a power and the logistic equation contains $P^2$. The other two are straight lines.

questions.prompt: Demand is $q = 1000 - 20p$. At what price $p$ (in pounds) is revenue $R = pq$ maximised?
A linear model that fits past data very well can still give poor predictions far outside the range of that data.
questions.explanation: Many real relationships are only approximately linear over a limited range. Extrapolation can break down when saturation or thresholds appear.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes the predator–prey term $\beta xy$ nonlinear?
options: It is a product of two variables
questions.explanation: A product of two variables means the effect of one depends on the level of the other, which breaks linearity.

questions.prompt: An energy tariff charges £0.30 per kWh for the first 200 kWh and £0.20 per kWh after that. Why is the bill a nonlinear function of usage?
options: Because electricity is measured in kWh
Because the rate changes at a threshold, putting a kink in the cost line
Because the bill is always more than £60
Because there is a standing charge
questions.explanation: A change of slope at 200 kWh makes the bill piecewise linear, which is nonlinear overall. A standing charge alone would still be linear (a constant term).

questions.prompt: What is the main practical advantage of linear models?
options: They are easy to solve, explain and combine, even with many variables
They can produce cycles and tipping points
questions.explanation: Linearity makes analysis and optimisation straightforward. Cycles and tipping points need nonlinear models.

concepts.title: Continuous vs discrete models
concepts.summary: Smooth change or step-by-step? Choosing between differential and difference equations.

blocks.md:
## Smooth or stepwise?

The continuous/discrete contrast can apply to **time** and to the **quantities** in a model.

**Continuous time**: the state changes at every instant, described by a differential equation:

$$\frac{dP}{dt} = rP \quad\Rightarrow\quad P(t) = P_0\,e^{rt}$$

**Discrete time**: the state jumps from one period to the next, described by a difference (recurrence) equation:

$$P_{n+1} = (1 + r)\,P_n \quad\Rightarrow\quad P_n = P_0\,(1 + r)^n$$

**Continuous quantities** can take any value (temperature, money, litres). **Discrete quantities** are whole numbers (customers, cars, hospital beds).

## How to choose

- Use **discrete time** when events really happen in steps: annual breeding seasons, monthly interest, weekly stock deliveries, data collected once a year.
- Use **continuous time** when change is ongoing and many small events overlap: drug elimination, chemical reactions, large populations, heat flow.
- Treating counts as continuous is fine when numbers are **large** (10,000 cars on a motorway). It is risky when numbers are **small** (3 ICU beds), where being off by one matters.

The two descriptions are closely linked: a difference equation with very small time steps approximates a differential equation. That is exactly how computers solve differential equations numerically.

blocks.title: Annual versus continuous compounding
blocks.problem: £1,000 is invested at 6% a year for 10 years. Compare the discrete model with annual compounding against the continuous model with continuous compounding.
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.**

Discrete: $B_{n+1} = 1.06\,B_n$, so $B_{10} = 1000 \times 1.06^{10}$.

Continuous: $\dfrac{dB}{dt} = 0.06B$, so $B(10) = 1000\,e^{0.06 \times 10} = 1000\,e^{0.6}$.

**Solve.**

$$B_{10} = 1000 \times 1.7908 \approx £1790.85$$

$$B(10) = 1000 \times 1.8221 \approx £1822.12$$

**Interpret.** Continuous compounding gives £31.27 more, because interest is added at every instant rather than once a year. The right model is the one that matches how the bank actually pays interest. For long horizons or high rates the difference grows, so the choice is not just cosmetic.

cards.back: Describes continuous-time change, e.g. $dP/dt = rP$.
Describes discrete-time change, e.g. $P_{n+1} = 1.05P_n$.
Takes whole-number values: patients, vehicles, orders.
Can take any value in a range: temperature, money, time.
The length of one period in a discrete model: a day, a month, a year.

items.q: Insects that breed once a year and then die. Continuous or discrete time?
items.a: Discrete. Generations do not overlap, so $N_{t+1} = f(N_t)$ matches the biology.

items.q: Caffeine leaving the bloodstream over an afternoon. Continuous or discrete time?
items.a: Continuous. Elimination happens all the time, so $dC/dt = -kC$ is natural.

items.q: Number of ambulances to station in a town. Continuous or discrete quantity?
items.a: Discrete. You cannot station 2.4 ambulances. Round answers sensibly, or use an integer model.

blocks.title: Rounding away small numbers
blocks.md: A continuous model says an optimal staffing level is 2.4 nurses. Rounding to 2 may leave the ward unsafe; rounding to 3 may break the budget. With small counts, check both neighbouring whole numbers in the real setting, or use a discrete (integer) model from the start.

questions.prompt: Which equation is a discrete-time model?
questions.explanation: A recurrence that updates from step $n$ to step $n+1$ is a discrete-time model. The others describe continuous change.

questions.prompt: A herd follows $P_{n+1} = 1.1\,P_n$ per year with $P_0 = 200$. What is $P_2$?
Continuous compounding at 6% a year gives a slightly larger balance after 10 years than annual compounding at 6%.
questions.explanation: $1000e^{0.6} \approx 1822.12$ compared with $1000 \times 1.06^{10} \approx 1790.85$.

questions.prompt: For which situation is treating a count as a continuous quantity most risky?
options: Daily vehicles on a busy motorway (about 80,000)
The number of ICU beds needed in a small rural hospital (around 3)
Annual passengers through a large airport
Litres of milk sold by a national supermarket chain
questions.explanation: With small counts, a fraction of a bed is meaningless and rounding errors change decisions. Large counts are well approximated as continuous.

questions.prompt: Which situations are naturally modelled in discrete time?
options: Annual breeding of a salmon population
Weekly stock deliveries to a shop
Caffeine leaving the bloodstream over an afternoon
questions.explanation: Repayments, breeding seasons and deliveries happen in steps. Heat flow and caffeine elimination are ongoing and suit continuous models.

concepts.title: Variables, parameters and constants
concepts.summary: Know which symbols you control, which you measure and which never change.

blocks.md:
## Different symbols, different jobs

Every symbol in a model plays a role. Mixing up roles is a common source of confused models.

- **Independent variable**: the input that is varied or that drives the model, often time $t$ or a decision such as price $p$.
- **Dependent variable**: the output that responds, such as profit, height or the number infected.
- **Parameters**: quantities held fixed **within** one scenario but which can differ **between** scenarios. They describe the particular situation, such as a growth rate, a price elasticity or a fuel efficiency. They are often estimated from data.
- **Constants**: fixed numbers that do not change between scenarios, such as $\pi$, or $g \approx 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$ near the Earth’s surface.

Two further roles you will meet constantly:

- **Decision variables**: inputs the modeller or manager controls (order size, number of staff).
- **State variables**: quantities that describe the system at a moment in a dynamic model (stock level, account balance).

## A labelled example

The height of a ball thrown upwards:

$$h(t) = h_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$$

Here $t$ is the independent variable, $h$ is the dependent variable, $h_0$ (launch height) and $v_0$ (launch speed) are parameters, and $g$ is a constant.

## Why the distinction matters

You **solve for** variables, **estimate** parameters and **look up** constants. Testing how outputs change when parameters change (sensitivity analysis) is one of the most useful things a model can do.

blocks.prompt: In the fuel-cost model $C = \dfrac{p}{e}\,d$ for a delivery van, match each symbol to its role.

blocks.title: Costing a delivery route
blocks.problem: A van does 12 km per litre and diesel costs £1.50 per litre. Write a model for the fuel cost of a route of $d$ km, find the cost of a 360 km route, and find the cost if the firm switches to a van doing 15 km per litre.
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** Litres used $= d/e$, so the cost is

$$C = \frac{p\,d}{e},$$

with independent variable $d$, dependent variable $C$, and parameters $p = 1.50$ and $e = 12$.

**Solve.**

$$C = \frac{1.50 \times 360}{12} = \frac{540}{12} = £45$$

With $e = 15$: $C = 540/15 = £36$.

**Interpret.** The route costs £45 in fuel; the more efficient van saves £9 per trip. Over 250 trips a year that is £2,250, which can be set against the cost of the new van. Changing a **parameter** and comparing outputs is exactly how models support decisions.

blocks.title: A parameter in one model is a variable in another
blocks.md: Roles depend on the **question**. For a driver planning today’s route, the fuel price $p$ is a fixed parameter. For a finance team studying how fuel prices affect annual costs, $p$ becomes an input they vary. Always state the role of each symbol for the question at hand.

blocks.question: In the logistic model $\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right)$ for a fish population, what is $K$?
blocks.explanation: $K$ is fixed for a given lake but differs between lakes, so it is a parameter. $t$ is independent and $P$ is dependent.

questions.prompt: In $h(t) = h_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$, which symbol is the dependent variable?
questions.explanation: Height $h$ responds to the input $t$; $h_0$ and $v_0$ are parameters and $g$ is a constant.

questions.prompt: A parameter is a quantity that is held fixed within one scenario but may take different values in different scenarios.
questions.explanation: That is what separates parameters from both variables (which change within a scenario) and constants (which never change).

questions.prompt: A van does 10 km per litre and fuel costs £1.60 per litre. What is the fuel cost, in pounds, of a 250 km route?
A café manager decides how many staff to roster each hour. In her staffing model, the number of staff is best described as…
questions.explanation: It is something she controls in order to influence the outcome, such as waiting times, which makes it a decision variable.

questions.prompt: In a savings model $S_{n+1} = (1 + i)S_n + d$, which statements are correct?
options: $d$ (the monthly deposit) is a universal constant
questions.explanation: The balance is the state, the rate is a parameter for this account, and $n$ indexes time. The deposit varies between savers, so it is a parameter or decision variable, not a universal constant.

concepts.title: Model assumptions and simplifications
concepts.summary: Leave out what doesn’t matter, and say clearly what you left out.

blocks.md:
## Why assume anything?

Reality has endless detail. A model that included everything would be impossible to build, solve or understand. **Assumptions** are the deliberate decisions about what to keep, what to ignore and what to treat as fixed. Good assumptions make a model tractable while keeping what matters for the question.

## Common types of assumption

- **Ignoring minor factors**: air resistance on a short throw, or the door and windows when estimating paint.
- **Constant rates**: prices, growth rates or costs stay the same over the period.
- **Homogeneity**: all customers, patients or machines behave alike.
- **Independence**: one customer’s arrival does not affect another’s.
- **Idealised shapes and behaviour**: a field is a rectangle, a pipe is a perfect cylinder, a market is perfectly competitive.

## What makes an assumption good?

1. **Explicit**: written down, not hidden.
2. **Justified**: supported by data, theory or a sensible argument.
3. **Appropriate to the question**: ignoring friction is fine for a rough estimate but not for designing brakes.
4. **Testable**: you can later relax it and see if the answer changes much.

A useful habit is to start simple, solve, then **relax one assumption at a time**. If the answer barely changes, the assumption was harmless. If it changes a lot, it was important and needs more care.

blocks.title: How much paint for a room?
blocks.problem: A room is 5 m long, 4 m wide and 2.5 m high. The walls need two coats, and one litre of paint covers 10 m². Estimate the paint needed, first ignoring the door and window, then allowing for a door of 2 m² and a window of 3 m².
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** Assumptions: walls are flat rectangles, coverage is exactly 10 m² per litre, the ceiling is not painted.

Wall area $= 2(\text{length} + \text{width}) \times \text{height}$. Paint (litres) $= \dfrac{2 \times \text{area}}{10}$.

**Solve.** Simple model: area $= 2(5 + 4) \times 2.5 = 45$ m², so paint $= 2 \times 45 / 10 = 9$ litres.

Relaxed model: area $= 45 - 2 - 3 = 40$ m², so paint $= 2 \times 40 / 10 = 8$ litres.

**Interpret.** Ignoring the door and window overestimates by 1 litre, about 12%. That error is on the safe side, since running out mid-job is worse than having a little left over, so the simple assumption is acceptable for buying paint. If you were pricing a large contract with hundreds of windows, you would need the more detailed model.

steps.title: List what could affect the output
steps.md: Brainstorm every factor, for example for delivery times: distance, traffic, weather, driver experience, parcel size, time of day.

steps.title: Rank by likely importance
steps.md: Distance and traffic matter most; parcel size matters little for a van.

steps.title: Decide: include, fix or ignore
steps.md: Include distance as a variable, fix average speed as a parameter (traffic folded in), ignore parcel size.

steps.title: Write each assumption explicitly
steps.md: "Average speed is 30 km/h throughout the day." "All parcels fit in one van."

steps.title: Plan how to test it
steps.md: Compare predictions with actual delivery logs; try a slower rush-hour speed and see how much the answer moves.

blocks.title: Hidden assumptions
blocks.md: The most dangerous assumptions are the ones nobody wrote down. Before the 2008 financial crisis, many mortgage risk models effectively assumed that house prices in different regions were unlikely to fall at the same time. When prices fell nationwide, losses were far larger than predicted. Listing assumptions explicitly is what allows others to challenge them.

items.q: A supermarket model assumes customers arrive at a constant rate all day. When might this fail?
items.a: At lunchtime and after work, when arrivals peak. Staffing based on the daily average would leave long queues at peak times.

items.q: An epidemic model assumes everyone mixes equally. What does that ignore?
items.a: Differences between age groups, households, schools and workplaces. It may get the overall scale right but miss where transmission is concentrated.

items.q: A profit model assumes all stock is sold. What is the effect?
items.a: It overstates profit whenever some stock is unsold, wasted or discounted.

blocks.question: You relax an assumption and the model’s answer barely changes. What does that tell you?
options: The assumption was wrong and must be removed
You need to add more assumptions
The output is not sensitive to it, so the simpler assumption is acceptable for this question
blocks.explanation: Low sensitivity means the simplification does little harm for this purpose.

questions.prompt: A good model includes every factor that could possibly affect the outcome.
questions.explanation: Good models keep only what matters for the question. Including everything makes a model impossible to build, solve or understand.

questions.prompt: Which is the best-written modelling assumption?
options: "Demand is constant at 400 units per week over the next quarter."
questions.explanation: It is explicit, specific and testable. The others are too vague to check or challenge.

questions.prompt: A room’s walls total 45 m². With two coats and coverage of 10 m² per litre, how many litres of paint are needed?
questions.explanation: $2 \times 45 / 10 = 9$ litres.

questions.prompt: Ignoring air resistance is a reasonable assumption for which situation?
options: Estimating how far a dropped phone falls from a desk
Calculating the top speed of a racing cyclist
Predicting the fall of a feather
questions.explanation: Over a short drop of a dense object, air resistance is negligible. In the other cases it is the dominant effect.

questions.prompt: Which are good practices when making assumptions?
options: Justifying assumptions with data or reasoning
Relaxing assumptions one at a time to test their impact
Keeping assumptions private so the model looks more accurate
Stating the conditions under which each assumption is reasonable
questions.explanation: Explicit, justified and tested assumptions, with their range of applicability stated, build trust. Hiding them prevents anyone from spotting a flaw.

questions.prompt: A simple model of a call centre assumes "all calls take the same time". Which type of assumption is this?
questions.explanation: Treating all calls as alike is a homogeneity assumption. In reality call lengths vary a lot, which affects waiting times.

concepts.title: Dimensional analysis and units
concepts.summary: Check any equation in seconds, and even guess its form, using units alone.

blocks.md:
## Units keep models honest

Every quantity in an applied model has **units**: pounds, kilometres, people per day. Checking units is the fastest way to catch errors in a model, and it can even suggest what form an equation should take.

## Dimensions

Units can be reduced to a few basic **dimensions**: mass $[M]$, length $[L]$, time $[T]$ (plus others such as temperature, or money and people in applied models). For example:

$$[\text{speed}] = L\,T^{-1}, \qquad [\text{acceleration}] = L\,T^{-2}, \qquad [\text{force}] = M\,L\,T^{-2}$$

## The principle of dimensional homogeneity

In a valid equation, **every term must have the same dimensions**. You can only add, subtract or equate like with like: metres plus metres, never metres plus seconds.

Two consequences:

- Rates carry "per time" units. In $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = rP$, $P$ is in people and $t$ in years, so $r$ must be in **per year** ($T^{-1}$).
- Inputs to functions such as $e^x$, $\ln x$ and $\sin x$ must be **dimensionless**. In $e^{rt}$, the product $rt$ has no units.

## Units in business and social models

The same logic applies to money and people: £ per unit times units gives £; customers per hour times hours gives customers. Ratios such as interest rates, percentages and elasticities are dimensionless, but rates still need a time unit: "5%" means nothing until you say per month or per year.

blocks.title: Finding the form of a pendulum law
blocks.problem: A clockmaker suspects that the period $T_p$ of a pendulum depends on its length $\ell$, the mass $m$ of the bob and gravitational acceleration $g$. Use dimensional analysis to find the form of the relationship, assuming $T_p = C\,\ell^a g^b m^c$ for a dimensionless constant $C$.
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** Dimensions: $[T_p] = T$, $[\ell] = L$, $[g] = L\,T^{-2}$, $[m] = M$. Homogeneity requires

$$T^1 = L^a\,(L\,T^{-2})^b\,M^c = L^{a+b}\,T^{-2b}\,M^c.$$

**Solve.** Match the powers of each dimension:

$$M:\ c = 0, \qquad T:\ -2b = 1 \Rightarrow b = -\tfrac{1}{2}, \qquad L:\ a + b = 0 \Rightarrow a = \tfrac{1}{2}.$$

So

$$T_p = C\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{g}}.$$

**Interpret.** Without any physics beyond units, we learn that the period does **not** depend on the mass, and that making the pendulum 4 times longer doubles its period. A full analysis gives $C = 2\pi$ for small swings. Dimensional analysis cannot find $C$, which is why experiments or theory are still needed.

blocks.title: The Mars Climate Orbiter
blocks.md: In 1999 NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one piece of software reported thruster impulse in pound-force seconds while another expected newton-seconds. The spacecraft’s trajectory was wrong and it was lost on arrival at Mars. In business models the equivalent errors are mixing monthly and annual rates, thousands and units, or pounds and euros. **Write units next to every number.**

steps.title: The claim
steps.md: A colleague models delivery time as $t = \dfrac{d}{v} + k\,n$, where $d$ is distance (km), $v$ is speed (km/h), $n$ is the number of stops and $k$ is a parameter.

steps.title: Units of the first term
steps.md: $d/v$ has units km ÷ (km/h) = hours. Good.

steps.title: What must $k$ be?
steps.md: For $k\,n$ to be in hours and $n$ to be a count, $k$ must be in **hours per stop**.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.md: The equation is homogeneous if $k$ is hours per stop, e.g. $k = 0.1$ (6 minutes a stop). If someone enters $k = 6$ thinking in minutes, the model is wrong by a factor of 60. Units tell you exactly where to look.

blocks.question: In the model $C(t) = C_0 e^{-kt}$ for drug concentration with $t$ in hours, what are the units of $k$?
options: It has no units because $t$ has units
blocks.explanation: The exponent $-kt$ must be dimensionless, so $k$ must be in per hour.

questions.prompt: In $\frac{dP}{dt} = rP$, $P$ is measured in people and $t$ in years. What are the units of $r$?
questions.explanation: $dP/dt$ is people per year and $P$ is people, so $r$ must be per year.

questions.prompt: An equation in which a length is added to a time can still be dimensionally valid if the numbers are small.
questions.explanation: Dimensional homogeneity requires every term to have the same dimensions, whatever the numerical values.

questions.prompt: Convert 72 km/h into metres per second.
With $s$ distance (m), $u$ speed (m/s), $a$ acceleration (m/s²) and $t$ time (s), which equation is dimensionally inconsistent?
questions.explanation: In $s = ut + at$, the term $at$ has units m/s, not m, so it cannot be added to a distance.

questions.prompt: Which of these quantities are dimensionless?
options: A growth rate of 3% per year
A delivery van’s speed in km per hour
questions.explanation: Elasticities and exponents are dimensionless. A growth rate "per year" has units of inverse time, and speed has units of length per time.

questions.prompt: Dimensional analysis shows that a pendulum’s period is proportional to $\sqrt{\ell/g}$. If the length is multiplied by 9, the period is multiplied by…
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{9} = 3$, so the period triples.

concepts.title: Model formulation and mathematical abstraction
concepts.summary: Strip a problem to its essential structure and build the equations step by step.

blocks.md:
## From situation to equations

**Formulation** is the step where a real problem becomes mathematics. **Abstraction** is the skill behind it: stripping away details until only the structure that matters is left.

## A formulation recipe

1. **State the question precisely.** Not "how is membership doing?" but "how many members will we have in 12 months?"
2. **Identify variables**: independent, dependent, decision and state variables, with units.
3. **List assumptions** about what to include, fix or ignore.
4. **Write the relationships**, often as a **balance law**:

$$\text{change} = \text{inflow} - \text{outflow}$$

5. **Add initial conditions and constraints.**
6. **Check** units, signs and limiting cases ("if nobody joins, does membership fall?").

## The power of abstraction

Once abstracted, very different problems share the same mathematics. The equation

$$\frac{dy}{dt} = -ky$$

describes radioactive decay, a drug leaving the bloodstream, a car losing value, and a cup of coffee cooling towards room temperature (with $y$ as the temperature difference). Solve it once and you have solved all of them. This is why mathematical modelling is a transferable skill across business, science and policy.

blocks.prompt: Put the formulation steps in a sensible order.
items: State the question precisely
Identify variables and their units
List assumptions
Write relationships as equations
Add initial conditions and constraints
Check units, signs and limiting cases

blocks.title: Forecasting gym membership
blocks.problem: A gym has 500 members. Each month about 40 people join and about 5% of existing members cancel. Formulate a model, find membership after 2 months, and find the long-run level. The owner wants 1,000 members: what would need to change?
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** Let $M_n$ be members after $n$ months. Assume the joining and cancellation rates stay constant. Balance law: next month $=$ this month $-$ cancellations $+$ joiners:

$$M_{n+1} = M_n - 0.05M_n + 40 = 0.95M_n + 40, \qquad M_0 = 500.$$

**Solve.**

$$M_1 = 0.95 \times 500 + 40 = 515, \qquad M_2 = 0.95 \times 515 + 40 = 529.25$$

Long run: at equilibrium $M^* = 0.95M^* + 40$, so $0.05M^* = 40$ and $M^* = 800$.

**Interpret.** Membership grows, but ever more slowly, towards about 800. To reach 1,000 members the gym needs $0.05 \times 1000 = 50$ joiners a month at 5% churn, or at 40 joiners it must cut churn to $40/1000 = 4\%$. The abstract equilibrium $M^* = \text{joiners} / \text{churn rate}$ turns a marketing debate into two concrete targets.

blocks.prompt: Each situation below has the same structure, $y_{n+1} = a\,y_n + b$. Match the meaning of $b$.

pairs.right: Fish restocked each year (negative if harvested)
Monthly repayment (entered as a negative amount)

blocks.title: Forgetting a flow
blocks.md: The most common formulation error is leaving out an inflow or outflow: modelling sign-ups but not cancellations, births but not deaths, sales but not returns. Before solving, list **every** way the quantity can increase and decrease, then check each appears in the equation with the correct sign.

questions.prompt: Which balance law underlies many formulation problems?
questions.explanation: A stock increases by what flows in and decreases by what flows out.

questions.prompt: A subscription service follows $M_{n+1} = 0.9M_n + 30$. What is its long-run (equilibrium) number of members?
questions.explanation: At equilibrium $M^* = 0.9M^* + 30$, so $0.1M^* = 30$ and $M^* = 300$.

questions.prompt: The equation $\frac{dy}{dt} = -ky$ can describe both a drug leaving the bloodstream and a car’s value depreciating.
questions.explanation: Both are processes where the rate of decrease is proportional to the current amount. Abstraction reveals the shared structure.

questions.prompt: A gym has $M_0 = 500$ members, 40 joiners a month and 5% monthly churn. What is $M_1$?
Which are sensible checks once a model has been formulated?
options: Signs make sense (e.g. cancellations reduce membership)
Limiting cases behave sensibly (e.g. no joiners means membership falls)
The model gives the answer the manager hoped for
questions.explanation: Units, signs and limiting cases catch formulation errors. Agreeing with a hoped-for answer is not a test of correctness.

questions.prompt: What does abstraction mean in mathematical modelling?
options: Making the model as detailed as possible
Removing inessential detail to expose the underlying mathematical structure
Copying a model from another field without checking it
questions.explanation: Abstraction keeps the essential structure, which is what makes models transferable between contexts.

concepts.title: Model calibration and validation
concepts.summary: Tune a model to data, then test it on data it has never seen.

blocks.md:
## Two different jobs

- **Calibration** (parameter estimation) chooses parameter values so that the model matches observed data as closely as possible.
- **Validation** tests whether the calibrated model predicts **new** data that was **not** used for calibration.

A model that fits the data it was tuned on has only passed calibration. Trust comes from validation.

## Measuring fit

The **residual** for each data point is the observed value minus the model’s prediction:

$$e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$$

Common summaries:

$$\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} |e_i|, \qquad \text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2}$$

**Least squares** calibration picks parameters that minimise the sum of squared residuals $\sum e_i^2$.

## Good practice

- **Split the data**: calibrate on one part (for example the first 18 months) and validate on the rest (the last 6).
- **Look at the residuals**, not just one score: a pattern such as all positive in winter means the model is missing something systematic.
- **Prefer simple models** unless extra complexity clearly improves validation performance. A model with many parameters can fit noise (**overfitting**) and then predict badly.
- Validation is **for a purpose**: a model can be valid for monthly budgeting but not for daily staffing.

blocks.title: Calibrating and validating a cost model
blocks.problem: A small manufacturer believes monthly cost follows $C = a + bq$, where $q$ is units produced. In January it made 100 units at a cost of £2,300; in February, 160 units at £2,900. Calibrate $a$ and $b$, then validate using March: 130 units, actual cost £2,650.
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** Two data points give two equations:

$$a + 100b = 2300, \qquad a + 160b = 2900.$$

**Solve.** Subtracting: $60b = 600$, so $b = 10$. Then $a = 2300 - 1000 = 1300$. The model is $C = 1300 + 10q$.

Validation, March: $\hat{C} = 1300 + 10 \times 130 = 2600$. The residual is $2650 - 2600 = 50$, an error of $50/2650 \approx 1.9\%$.

**Interpret.** Fixed costs are about £1,300 a month and each unit adds about £10. The model predicted unseen data within 2%, which is encouraging, but one validation point is thin evidence: the manager should keep comparing predictions with actual costs each month. Note that with only two calibration points the line fits January and February **exactly**, so the fit to those months tells us nothing about accuracy.

steps.title: Split the data
steps.md: Keep a hold-out set that the model never sees during calibration, for example the most recent 25% of observations.

steps.title: Calibrate
steps.md: Choose parameters to minimise error (for example least squares) on the calibration set only.

steps.title: Predict the hold-out set
steps.md: Run the calibrated model forward and compare with the held-out observations.

steps.title: Measure and inspect
steps.md: Compute MAE or RMSE and plot the residuals over time to look for patterns.

steps.title: Decide
steps.md: If validation error is acceptable for the purpose, use the model. If not, revisit assumptions or structure, not just the parameters.

blocks.title: Validating on the calibration data
blocks.md: Reporting how well a model fits the same data it was tuned on is like marking your own exam with the answer sheet open. A ten-parameter curve can pass through ten sales figures perfectly and still forecast next month terribly. Always hold some data back.

blocks.question: A model’s predictions for three weeks have residuals of 2, −1 and 3 units. What is the mean absolute error?

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between calibration and validation?
options: Calibration uses more data than validation
Validation estimates parameters; calibration checks units
Calibration estimates parameters from data; validation tests predictions on data not used for calibration
questions.explanation: Calibration tunes the model; validation tests it on independent data.

questions.prompt: Residuals are 2, −1 and 3. What is the mean absolute error (MAE)?
A model that fits its calibration data perfectly is guaranteed to predict new data well.
questions.explanation: A perfect fit can come from overfitting noise. Only validation on unseen data shows predictive ability.

questions.prompt: Using two months of data, a cost model is calibrated as $C = 1300 + 10q$. What cost does it predict for $q = 180$ units?
The residuals of a sales model are positive every December and negative every February. What does this suggest?
options: The model is missing a systematic seasonal effect
questions.explanation: A regular pattern in residuals means the model systematically misses something, here seasonality.

questions.prompt: Which are good practices in validating a forecasting model?
options: Holding back recent data that is not used for calibration
Plotting residuals to look for patterns
Choosing whichever model has the most parameters
Reporting accuracy only on the calibration data
Re-tuning the parameters on the hold-out data until its error is zero
questions.explanation: Hold-out data and residual checks are good practice. More parameters often means overfitting; accuracy on calibration data says little about prediction; and tuning on the hold-out data destroys its value as an independent test.

concepts.title: Limitations and interpretation of mathematical models
concepts.summary: All models are wrong, some are useful. Learn to read results with care.

blocks.md:
## "All models are wrong, but some are useful"

The statistician George Box’s famous remark sums up this lesson. A model is a tool for a purpose, not a statement of truth. Interpreting it well means knowing **where it can be trusted, how uncertain it is, and what it cannot tell you**.

## Main sources of limitation

- **Domain of validity**: a model is only reliable in the range of conditions it was built and tested for. Outside it you are **extrapolating**.
- **Assumptions**: every simplification is a possible point of failure.
- **Parameter uncertainty**: parameters estimated from limited, noisy data have error bars.
- **Structural uncertainty**: the form of the model itself may be wrong.
- **Sensitivity**: if a small change in an input produces a large change in the output, the result is fragile.
- **Correlation is not causation**: an empirical model can predict from a relationship without explaining it. Changing the input on purpose may not change the output.

## Sensitivity in one line

A simple way to measure sensitivity is to change one input by a small percentage and see the percentage change in the output:

$$\text{sensitivity} \approx \frac{\%\ \text{change in output}}{\%\ \text{change in input}}$$

## Interpreting and communicating

- Report results as **ranges or scenarios**, not single falsely precise numbers.
- State the key assumptions and what would change the conclusion.
- Remember that models **support** decisions; people still weigh values, ethics and factors the model leaves out.
- Be aware that a widely used model can change the behaviour it predicts: a published forecast of shortages can itself cause panic buying.

blocks.title: How fragile is the profit forecast?
blocks.problem: A product sells for £10, costs £6 per unit to make, and fixed costs are £15,000. Forecast sales are 5,000 units. Find the forecast profit, then find the profit if the unit cost rises by 10%. What should the analyst tell the board?
blocks.solution:
**Formulate.** Profit $= (p - c)\,q - F$ with $p = 10$, $c = 6$, $q = 5000$, $F = 15000$.

**Solve.** Base case:

$$(10 - 6) \times 5000 - 15000 = 20000 - 15000 = £5000$$

Unit cost up 10% to £6.60:

$$(10 - 6.60) \times 5000 - 15000 = 17000 - 15000 = £2000$$

A 10% rise in one input cuts profit by 60%, a sensitivity of about $60/10 = 6$.

**Interpret.** The single figure "£5,000 profit" hides how fragile it is. The analyst should present a range ("between £2,000 and £5,000 depending on input costs"), flag unit cost as the critical input, and suggest securing a fixed-price supply contract. Interpreting a model includes saying which assumptions the answer leans on most.

items.q: Where does this model come from, and what was it built for?
items.a: A model built for monthly national averages may not suit daily local decisions.

items.q: What are the key assumptions, and are they still true?
items.a: A demand model calibrated before a competitor entered the market may now be out of date.

items.q: Am I inside the range of the data?
items.a: Predicting sales at a price never tried before is extrapolation, so treat it with extra caution.

items.q: How sensitive is the answer?
items.a: Vary the uncertain inputs. If the decision flips with small changes, gather better data before acting.

items.q: Is this relationship causal?
items.a: Ice cream sales and sunburn cases rise together, but banning ice cream would not prevent sunburn. Both are driven by sunny weather.

blocks.title: Extrapolation and false precision
blocks.md: A trend line through three months of sales (200, 220, 240) predicts 1,380 units in month 60. Nothing in three months of data supports a five-year forecast. Reporting "1,380" rather than a wide range implies a confidence the model does not have. **Precision is not accuracy.**

blocks.question: A model of house prices was calibrated on data from a period of low interest rates. A planner uses it to forecast prices after a sharp rise in rates. What is the main concern?
options: The model has too few decimal places
The model is being used outside its domain of validity
blocks.explanation: The relationships learned under low rates may not hold under very different conditions: an extrapolation outside the calibration range.

questions.prompt: If a model has been validated once, its predictions can be trusted under any future conditions.
questions.explanation: Validation applies to the conditions tested. If circumstances change, such as a new competitor, a policy change or a shock, the model may no longer be valid.

questions.prompt: Profit is $(p - c)q - F$ with $p = £10$, $c = £6$, $q = 5000$ and $F = £15{,}000$. What is the profit if the unit cost rises to £6.60?
Cities with more fire engines report more fire damage. A model uses fire engines to predict damage well. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Fire engines cause fire damage, so cities should buy fewer
The relationship is likely driven by a common factor such as city size, so it does not show that fire engines cause damage
Fire damage causes cities to have fewer fire engines
questions.explanation: Correlation is not causation. Larger cities have both more engines and more fires; the model can predict without explaining.

questions.prompt: Which are good ways to communicate a model’s results?
options: Giving a range or several scenarios
Highlighting which inputs the result is most sensitive to
Reporting a single figure to many decimal places to look authoritative
questions.explanation: Ranges, assumptions and sensitivities give decision-makers an honest picture. Excess decimal places create false precision.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures George Box’s view of models?
options: All models are wrong, but some are useful
A good model is exactly right
Models are only useful if they include every factor
Complex models are always better than simple ones
questions.explanation: Box’s remark stresses that models are simplifications whose value lies in usefulness for a purpose.

questions.prompt: A 10% rise in unit cost cuts profit from £5,000 to £2,000. By what percentage does profit fall?
questions.explanation: The fall is £3,000, and $3000 / 5000 = 0.6$, which is 60%.

sections.objective: Develop the mathematical foundations required to construct and analyse models.
competencies: Select appropriate mathematical functions for modelling

concepts.title: Algebraic expressions and equations
concepts.summary: Turn a business question into symbols, then solve for the number that answers it.

blocks.title: Level 2: Mathematical Tools for Modelling
blocks.md:
Develop the mathematical foundations required to construct and analyse models.
